items.title: How Loopjacking Hijacks Human Approval in AI Workflows
items.author: OffSec
items.content:
Imagine an AI agent asks you to approve a small payment to a familiar vendor. You check the amount, verify the recipient, and approve it.

The workflow continues. A much larger payment goes to a different destination.

You return to the approval record. It still contains the original request.

This scenario illustrates : a failure in which software uses a human’s approval for one operation to authorize or release something materially different. The experiments discussed here used harmless mock transfers and local recording tools; no money moved.

The uncomfortable part is that the human can make the correct decision. The software fails to preserve what that decision authorized.

Researcher Adithyan Arun Kumar examines this gap in . The study distinguishes two ways it can happen: an operation changes after approval, or the approval view leaves out consequential details that were present all along. Both break the same expectation: what you approve should be what executes.

What a click on “Approve” actually authorizes

When someone approves a payment, they approve an amount and a recipient. For a file upload, the destination and files matter. For a command, its arguments and execution context can change its consequences.

An agent workflow has to carry that meaning through several components. One proposes an action. Another prepares the approval view. The workflow may pause, save its state, and resume later. Eventually, a tool performs the operation.

The security requirement extends across that entire path. A record saying “this task was approved” cannot establish that every later action within the task was approved. Even the same tool-call identifier can refer to changed arguments if the implementation permits replacement.

For an attacker, that distinction can create an opportunity: influence the operation while retaining someone else’s authorization.

A qualifying Loopjacking case therefore requires a genuine approval, a materially different effect outside its scope, and a reachable way for an attacker to make the product consume that approval. The attacker must also lack an equivalent direct route to the effect.

When the action changes after approval

State substitution starts with an accurate request. The reviewer sees operation A and approves it. Before execution, attacker-influenced workflow state substitutes operation B, and the system continues using the earlier decision.

The study’s Agno AgentOS experiment makes this concrete. Its tested regular-Agent configuration separated two roles: a lower-privileged user could initiate and continue a run, while a distinct administrator could approve the proposed operation.

The approved operation was a mock transfer of 20 units to an approved vendor. The operation ultimately dispatched was a mock transfer of 2,000 units to a different destination.

The lower-privileged user could neither approve the request nor directly execute the substituted operation. Yet after the administrator approved the original request, the product accepted changed continuation data and dispatched the different transfer. The approval record still described the original operation.

In the recorded Agno bundle, this mismatch occurred in five of five trials. Unchanged approved operations executed in five of five controls, while all three direct attempts at the substituted operation were denied. These results apply to the exact tested configuration; they do not measure how frequently deployed systems are affected. The public evidence index documents the boundaries and controls.

An additional researcher-built control compared the approved operation with the operation about to execute. It rejected the substitution while allowing the original transfer. That demonstrates a working defense for the tested path, rather than a released Agno fix.

When the approval view leaves something out

Representation mismatch starts with an incomplete view. No change after approval is necessary. The consequential behavior is already encoded in the request, but the approval view does not faithfully represent it.

A previously disclosed OpenClaw issue demonstrates this distinction. In the affected command-execution path, approval text could represent only part of a shell command’s execution context. Additional arguments consumed at runtime were absent from that representation.

The vendor’s security advisory, which credits the original reporter, describes the mismatch and identifies as the patched release.

Kumar’s study reproduced the mismatch on using a harmless temporary marker. The same mismatch was rejected on , while unchanged approved commands continued to work. The approval role was scripted after recording and checking the exact product event: the experiment measured system behavior, not whether people would be deceived by a particular interface. The OpenClaw evidence record preserves that distinction.

This explains why freezing a request after approval is an incomplete defense. An immutable request can still be inadequately represented to its reviewer.

A control that kept approval intact

The study also included an implementation that preserved the approval boundary. In OpenAI Agents SDK and , ordinary per-call approval remained bound to the invocation across saving and restoring workflow state. Unchanged approved operations executed; changed invocation arguments retaining the call identifier were rejected.

For each release, all three unchanged-operation controls passed, and all three mutation trials were rejected without a recorded effect. The negative-control evidence applies to the tested ordinary per-call approval path, not every approval mode or application built around the SDK.

That result matters because agent workflows need to pause and resume. Persistence and continuation can coexist with meaningful approval. The implementation has to preserve the operation-specific authorization through those transitions.

Where prompt injection fits

Prompt injection can influence what an agent proposes or place attacker-controlled content into a workflow. Loopjacking concerns the subsequent authorization failure: an implementation consumes a human decision for an operation outside its scope. The two can occur together, but Loopjacking does not require prompt injection.

Loopjacking groups concrete approval-to-effect failures in agent workflows and distinguishes how they arise. It does not imply that approval integrity is a newly discovered security principle, or that all agent frameworks share one vulnerability.

What developers should preserve through execution

For developers, the practical requirement is to make the approval interface and execution system agree on the operation being authorized. Four design choices help make that agreement enforceable:

  1. Build the approval view from the operation that will execute. Include the arguments, destination, resources, and context that materially affect the outcome. A readable summary can help, but it cannot replace consequential details.
  2. Bind the decision to a protected operation record. Preserve what was approved, who approved it, and the scope and validity of that decision. A task identifier or an “approved” flag is insufficient when the operation underneath it can change.
  3. Compare again immediately before execution. Resolve the current operation and check it against the approved record. A material change should stop execution or require fresh approval. Protect the checked operation against further substitution before dispatch.
  4. Make approval consumption and audit records precise. Enforce expiry and reuse limits, and record both the approved operation and the operation actually released. Retries should not silently expand what a one-time decision permits.

A cryptographic digest can help bind these records, but only if it covers the relevant operation and is protected from tampering. Hashing an incomplete description preserves the same omission.

For teams evaluating their own workflows, a useful acceptance test is whether unchanged approved operations succeed while materially different operations require a new decision. The evidence should include the actual effect at the tool boundary; a successful response or an approval entry alone cannot establish that the correct action executed.

The study used isolated environments, synthetic identities, and harmless recording tools, with an evidence cutoff of September 10, 2026. It establishes specific implementation failures and working controls. It does not establish ecosystem prevalence, and independent reproduction is not claimed.

For a person reviewing an action, approval carries a concrete meaning. The software’s job is to preserve it through execution. An audit trail should show who authorized which operation, and that the operation released stayed within that authorization.

items.title: Cloudflare Keeps 1.1.1.1 Out of Piracy Blocking, Escapes Penalties In France
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Cloudflare doesn't block pirate sports streaming sites through its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver in France, only through its CDN. The Paris Judicial Court has now accepted that stance, rejecting [French pay-TV provider] Canal+'s request for penalties of 50,000 euros per site, per day. Interestingly, the court's conclusion relies on statistics provided by Canal+ itself. [...] As a result, Cloudflare will not be penalized under these orders, even though its public DNS resolver is not blocking the sites in question. That is in line with the company's long-standing claim that it doesn't interfere with its DNS.
 
In its recent transparency reports, Cloudflare repeatedly stated that it hasn't blocked any content through 1.1.1.1, despite orders from French and Italian courts. "To date, Cloudflare has not blocked content through the 1.1.1.1 Public DNS Resolver," the company's latest report reads. [...] Blocking through the CDN is another matter. According to the same report, Cloudflare geoblocked 1,238 domains in France in the second half of 2025, all under a single court order. In the first half of the year, it geoblocked 662 domains under seven orders. Cloudflare recently explained its position to the European Commission, in a submission (PDF) to its Counterfeit and Piracy Watch List consultation, stressing that global public DNS resolvers should not be used to block or restrict access.
 
Instead, it highlights its real-time pirate stream blocking program, which allows vetted rightsholders to flag pirate streams that run through its network. These streams are disrupted "within seconds," Cloudflare says, without any DNS or IP address blocking. "For live content, where speed is crucial, Cloudflare has built real-time mitigation mechanisms that allow vetted rightsholder partners to flag infringing streams. When those streams are running through our network, we act on them in seconds," Cloudflare informed the Commission. For now, Cloudflare can continue to block pirate sites through its CDN only, while its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver remains untouched. Canal+ can still appeal the rulings, so it may not be the last we hear of it.

items.title: How David Bratslavsky Is Helping Commercial Real Estate Operators Use AI to Win Deals
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Multifamily sales volume reached $22.8 billion in the first quarter of 2026. Deal velocity is climbing. Capital is moving. And at most investment firms, the bottleneck is not sourcing or financing. It is the hours an acquisitions team spends transferring numbers from rent rolls and operating statements into Excel before anyone can run a single projection.

built QuickData.ai to eliminate that transfer step. The platform is an Excel add-in that reads multifamily financial documents and places the extracted data directly into whatever underwriting model the firm already uses. The company reports 99.3% accuracy on rent-roll extraction and identification rate for trailing twelve-month operating statement line items. More than 800 multifamily professionals use the tool, according to the company, at $99 per user per month.

That product was the starting point. What followed was a consulting practice that now helps commercial real estate firms build AI capabilities across their operations.

A Speed Problem With a Dollar Value

For a multifamily investor evaluating twenty or thirty acquisition opportunities per month, underwriting speed has a direct relationship to deal flow coverage. Every property requires the same preparation: pull the rent roll data, categorize the T12 expenses, normalize the offering memorandum figures, and populate the firm's financial model. The mechanical portion of that work, the part that involves reading a PDF and typing numbers into cells, accounts for the majority of the time an analyst spends before the actual evaluation begins.

"QuickData helps multifamily professionals underwrite deals 10x faster by automating rent roll, T12, and OM data entry into Excel," said David Bratslavsky, founder of QuickData.ai, describing the product's core function.

Users save an average of 15 hours per month, according to QuickData.ai. For a three-person acquisitions team, that represents 45 hours redirected from data entry to deal evaluation. In a market where the firm that completes its underwriting first is often the firm that controls the negotiation, those hours carry a measurable cost when wasted and a measurable advantage when recovered.

The tool was trained specifically on multifamily document formats, according to the company, which is why generic document-processing software tends to produce unreliable results in this sector. A rent roll from one property management company categorises charges differently than one from another. T12 line items vary by operator. Offering memorandums follows no standard layout. The extraction engine was built to handle those inconsistencies rather than guess through them.

Working with investment firms on the underwriting problem, Bratslavsky saw that rent-roll extraction was one instance of a pattern that repeated across the entire business. Leasing teams read lease amendments to track critical dates. Asset managers compile monthly reports to explain budget variances. Investor relations teams turn portfolio data into quarterly updates. Each of these tasks involves finding, organising, checking, and moving information from one place to another.

That recognition led Bratslavsky to build a consulting practice around what he describes as AI skills: reusable sets of instructions, trained on a firm's own documents and terminology, that handle specific repetitive tasks. One skill might categorize operating expenses. Another might reconcile conflicting figures across documents. A third might populate a quarterly investor report from reviewed data.

The consulting engagements follow a consistent structure. Bratslavsky works with the firm's employees to identify a task, document how it currently works, build an AI skill that replicates it, and test the output against real documents. The employees learn the process so they can maintain and extend the automations after the engagement ends.

The practice now works with multifamily, office, and industrial firms, brokers, and lenders, applying the same method to lease abstraction, asset management reporting, and covenant monitoring. Bratslavsky, who has worked as a fractional chief technology officer, brings a background that combines technology operations with real estate investing.

The investor who evaluates forty opportunities per month and the investor who evaluates fifteen are not equally positioned, even if their judgment is identical. The difference is coverage. When underwriting preparation takes less time, more properties get a full evaluation instead of a preliminary screen and a pass.

QuickData.ai addresses the mechanical layer of that preparation. The consulting practice addresses the organisational layer: teaching firms to apply AI to the other repetitive tasks that accumulate across acquisitions, asset management, and investor reporting. Together, they represent Bratslavsky's answer to a question that most multifamily firms are asking in some form: how do you increase deal coverage without proportionally increasing headcount?

The answer, in his framing, is not to replace the people doing the work. It is to remove the hours they spend on tasks that do not require their expertise, and let them apply that time to the decisions that do.

items.title: The Lawyer Who's Building His Own Version Of Legal AI
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Daman Singh Saduara didn't set out to compete with Westlaw. He set out to be a lawyer.

Saduara trained in law at the University of Leicester, completed an LLM at the University of Miami, and interned with Aliette Rodriguez's team at Shutts & Bowen in Miami, one of the country's largest firms. Everything about that path pointed toward a bar exam and a career inside a major legal practice. He chose not to sit the exam. Instead, he built , an AI automation and consulting company, in Miami in January 2026, with his brother, Gurvir Singh Saduara, as co-founder. Gurvir studied mechanical engineering and 3D robotics at Conestoga College in Kitchener-Waterloo, a technical background that now feeds directly into how the two of them approach product development.

Now Saduara is turning that same instinct toward an industry he knows from the inside: legal services.

What law school actually taught him

"Everything I learned in law, I'm using now," Saduara said. "I just don't have to ask permission to build with it." For a founder without a computer science background, that's not a throwaway line. It's the whole thesis behind everything he's built since.

Saduara credits Marike Paulson, one of his professors, with pushing him to publish early in his academic career, an exercise he says forced him to think clearly in writing before he ever tried explaining an idea out loud. Howard Kwon taught him how to integrate AI into daily workflows inside an actual law firm setting, which turned out to be a preview of exactly the kind of problem Saduara is now trying to solve at scale, years before he had a company to apply it to. A separate memory stuck just as hard. Daniel Gonzalez and Mark Cheskin, partners at Hogan Lovells in Miami, once mentioned in passing a former student who'd gone on to become a client of their own firm. Saduara says it completely reframed how he thought about ambition. The goal was never just landing a job at a top firm. It was becoming the kind of person a top firm would want as a client.

That reframing is now the business plan, aimed at an entire industry rather than a single career.

Two products, one very specific problem

Saduara's newest venture is , an AI company he owns that builds tools spanning websites, ad campaigns across Meta, Snapchat, LinkedIn, and X, and AI-generated content for companies and brands that want a presence without a full production team. Its first two products both target the legal industry directly, and they're built to solve different versions of the same underlying problem: every law firm works differently, and most existing tools don't account for that.

Hawk is a plug-and-play legal research and writing tool, positioned as a direct alternative to Westlaw and LexisNexis. Saduara describes it in blunt terms: purchase it, plug it into your existing workflow, done. No custom integration, no months-long onboarding process, no retraining an entire department on a new system. It's built for firms that want the capability without the operational lift.

Hawk 2.0 takes the opposite approach. It's a fully white-label, enterprise-level platform built specifically for law firms that want to shape the tool around themselves rather than adapt to someone else's design. Name, automation logic, feature set, even the interface, all of it is customizable. Where Hawk is meant to slot into a firm's existing process without disruption, Hawk 2.0 is meant to eventually become the firm's process.

"Every law firm does legal research and legal writing differently," Saduara said. "Most tools ask firms to adapt to one fixed system. We're building the opposite, something that adapts to them."

Betting on the firms that already know what good looks like

Saduara isn't planning a wide public launch out of the gate, and he's direct about why. He wants Hawk tested first at the University of Leicester and the University of Miami, the two schools where he studied, with trials aimed specifically at finding bugs and stress-testing the tool in a real academic legal environment before it goes anywhere near a paying client. It's a deliberate choice to start with institutions he trusts and that already operate to rigorous standards, rather than opening access broadly and hoping the product holds up under pressure.

Hawk 2.0 is targeted for an early 2027 release, with the base Hawk platform following in mid to late 2027. The sequencing reflects how Saduara is thinking about risk. Enterprise clients working directly with his team on a customized build can absorb early iteration in a way a self-serve product can't, so the more controlled release comes first, and the plug-and-play version follows once the underlying system has been tested against real firm demands.

Both his own credibility and Loophole's are staked on the tool working the way it's supposed to from day one, not on being first to market. "I'm not building this because I left law behind," Saduara said. "I'm building it because I didn't."

For a founder who walked away from a conventional legal career specifically to avoid being boxed into one way of operating, building a legal AI platform designed around flexibility isn't ironic. It's the same instinct, aimed at a different industry, built on the same conviction that no two law firms or careers should have to fit the same mold.

THE CURSE OF RESOLUTION IN PHYSICS SIMULATIONS

Imagine watching water flow through sand at two different zoom levels. At low zoom, you see the overall current pushing through the domain. At high zoom, individual sand grains create turbulence and complex flow patterns that wouldn't be visible from far away. To capture both, you need the high-zoom video, which takes forever to compute. Yet you can't simply use the low-zoom version because those tiny grain-scale interactions fundamentally change how the bulk flow behaves.

This is the core tension in finite element methods, the standard tool scientists use to approximate solutions to the differential equations governing physical systems. In these methods, computational cost scales brutally with resolution. Double your resolution in two dimensions and you create 16 times more elements. In three dimensions, that's 64 times more. This isn't a problem you solve by throwing more compute at it indefinitely. High-resolution simulations are accurate but prohibitively expensive. Coarse simulations are fast but miss crucial small-scale details that ripple through the big picture.

The multiscale structures in physics aren't incidental; they're fundamental. Small-scale heterogeneity in materials, turbulent fluctuations in fluids, grain-boundary effects in crystals, all these phenomena affect macroscopic behavior in ways that can't simply be averaged away. Yet capturing them requires the computational horsepower of a high-resolution simulation, creating a genuine impasse between speed and accuracy.

WHY TRADITIONAL MULTISCALE METHODS DON'T QUITE SOLVE IT

Researchers have known for decades that you need something smarter than brute-force high-resolution simulation. The traditional approach looks like dividing a puzzle into pieces. You solve the problem at a coarse scale, figure out how that coarse solution influences the fine scale, then solve the fine-scale problem in each region, coupling the results back together. Mathematically, this works. Computationally, it's more involved than it sounds.

Methods like homogenization and multiscale finite element methods are mathematically rigorous and can provide guarantees about their approximations. But they require solving auxiliary problems, like the "cell problems" in homogenization theory, to understand how fine scales feed back into coarse scales. For complex materials or irregular geometries, these auxiliary problems can be nearly as expensive as the original simulation. You're trading one hard problem for several smaller hard problems, which is an improvement but not revolutionary.

The core limitation is that multiscale methods still require explicit computation of fine-scale corrections. You don't truly escape the resolution curse; you just distribute the work differently. For time-dependent problems or when you need to run many similar simulations, this overhead becomes prohibitive.

SUPER-RESOLUTION AS LEARNED MULTISCALE CORRECTION

What if you bypassed mathematical derivation entirely and instead let a neural network learn the relationship between coarse and fine scales from examples? You run many simulations at both coarse and fine resolution, showing the network thousands of pairs, and ask it to learn the underlying pattern. Then, for new problems, you run only the cheap coarse simulation and let the network fill in the fine details.

This reframes the multiscale problem fundamentally. Instead of asking "how do I mathematically derive the fine-scale correction from the coarse solution," you ask "what statistical relationship exists between coarse-resolution snapshots of physics and fine-resolution snapshots?" Train a network to learn that relationship, and it becomes a reusable tool.

The brilliant insight is that you don't need to hand-derive the multiscale coupling. You're leveraging an assumption about the physical world: that small-scale structures follow patterns that are learnable and repeatable across different scenarios. If those patterns truly reflect the underlying physics, the network should generalize beyond its training distribution. It should work on upsampling factors it never saw, on material properties it never explicitly trained on.

Continuous super-resolution bridges coarse and fine scales. The orange region shows in-distribution scenarios (upsampling factors up to 16x), while the blue region shows out-of-distribution tests where the method extrapolates to 32x and beyond. The orange region shows in-distribution scenarios (upsampling factors up to 16x), while the blue region shows out-of-distribution tests where the method extrapolates to 32x and beyond.

This is where the paper departs from typical deep learning applications. It's not just applying image super-resolution to scientific data. It's asking whether neural networks can learn and extrapolate the structure of multiscale physics.

THE ARCHITECTURE: LOCAL IMPLICIT TRANSFORMERS LEARN ACROSS SCALES

Building a network that handles both coarse context and fine reconstruction simultaneously requires solving a specific technical challenge. How do you make a neural network that respects multiscale structure, preserves both large-scale features and fine details, and works at arbitrary query locations, not just fixed grid points?

The answer involves two key components working in concert. First, local implicit neural representations (LIIF) treat space as continuous rather than discrete. Instead of the network learning a grid of pixel values, it learns a continuous function that can predict the field value at any spatial coordinate, like x=0.1234, y=0.5678. The coarse module processes the coarse finite element solution and extracts features. The fine module takes those features plus a query coordinate and outputs the fine-resolution prediction at that specific location.

Second, a transformer architecture handles the multiscale learning. Transformers excel at learning long-range dependencies and attention patterns, which maps directly to the physics: the fine-scale behavior at one location depends on coarse features potentially across a large region. The transformer learns which parts of the coarse domain matter for predicting details at any given location.

The architecture processes coarse finite element data through feature extraction, then uses a local implicit function in the transformer to predict fine-scale corrections at arbitrary spatial coordinates. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/network_v2.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/network_v2.jpg] The architecture processes coarse finite element data through feature extraction, then uses a local implicit function in the transformer to predict fine-scale corrections at arbitrary spatial coordinates.

The elegance of this design is that it separates the two jobs cleanly. The coarse module sees the big picture. The fine module handles spatial interpolation and detail generation. The transformer connects them by learning which coarse features to attend to for each fine-scale prediction.

THE FREQUENCY PROBLEM: WHY GABOR WAVELETS FIX NEURAL NETWORK BLINDNESS

Here's a subtle but critical problem that most practitioners would miss. Neural networks are biased learners. When you show them spatial data and ask them to predict values, they naturally learn smooth, low-frequency features first. Their internal "perception" gravitates toward blurry versions of the input. For multiscale corrections, this is backwards. You desperately need the network to pay serious attention to high-frequency details that create the fine structure.

This isn't a failure of the network; it's a feature of how they learn. Low-frequency functions are often the "easy" solution that reduces loss quickly and smoothly. Standard positional encodings help somewhat, but the paper proposes something more targeted: Gabor wavelets as coordinate encodings.

Gabor functions are sinusoidal waves modulated by a Gaussian envelope, and they're particularly good at capturing localized frequency structure. By encoding the spatial coordinates using Gabor wavelets instead of simple sinusoids, the network gets a built-in curriculum that encourages it to respect fine-scale structure from the start. It's like giving the network glasses that make high-frequency details visually prominent.

The impact is visible in frequency-space analysis. Using radial power spectral density (RAPSD), you can decompose how much energy the predicted field contains at each frequency scale.

Frequency analysis via radial power spectral density (RAPSD) shows that the proposed method preserves high-frequency content that simpler approaches lose, matching the ground truth spectrum more closely. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/rapsd_compare.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/rapsd_compare.jpg] Frequency analysis via radial power spectral density (RAPSD) shows that the proposed method preserves high-frequency content that simpler approaches lose, matching the ground truth spectrum more closely.

The proposed method maintains the correct frequency spectrum. Competitors without this frequency-aware encoding produce outputs that are systematically too smooth, missing the sharp transitions and fine textures that characterize physical fields.

COMPARING PATCHES INSTEAD OF PIXELS: STOCHASTIC COSINE SIMILARITY

If you want a neural network to produce physically realistic fine details, you can't just compare its prediction to ground truth pixel-by-pixel. A pixel-level loss function like mean squared error will push the network toward a blurry average of many possible fine structures, which looks wrong to human eyes and doesn't capture the structural patterns of real physical fields. The paper recognizes that "perception is often preferred over distortion," meaning scientists care whether the fine-scale pattern looks and behaves like real physics, not just whether numbers match exactly.

The solution is stochastic cosine similarity (SCS), which compares local regions (patches) rather than individual points. Instead of asking "does prediction[pixel i] match ground_truth[pixel i]?", it asks "does the pattern of features in prediction[region j] match the pattern in ground_truth[region j]?" Cosine similarity measures how aligned two vectors are in direction, ignoring their magnitude. This encourages the network to get the structure right even if it's shifted slightly or scaled differently. Stochastic means you sample random patches during training, giving the network diverse supervision across the domain.

Training curves show that incorporating stochastic cosine similarity loss improves convergence and final reconstruction quality compared to standard pixel-level losses. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/loss_curve.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/loss_curve.jpg] Training curves show that incorporating stochastic cosine similarity loss improves convergence and final reconstruction quality compared to standard pixel-level losses.

This is a subtle but important detail that bridges the gap between mathematical accuracy and visual/structural fidelity. A network optimized only for pixel-level MSE will produce outputs that look blurry but have low numerical error. A network optimized with SCS learns to preserve the local structure and patterns that make the field look physically plausible to human inspection and domain-expert evaluation.

IN-DISTRIBUTION VERSUS OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION: HOW FAR CAN THE PATTERN GENERALIZE

There's a critical question hidden in every learning-based approach to scientific computing: how much can the network actually generalize? If you train on simulations with upsampling factor up to 16x, can it handle 32x? If you train on one type of material coefficient, can it work on completely different physical scenarios?

The distinction matters enormously. Any neural network can memorize training data. The real test of whether you've learned a physics-driven pattern, rather than just captured statistical artifacts of your training set, is whether it works on new configurations and extrapolation scenarios.

The experiments are structured to test both regimes carefully. The network trains on coarse-fine pairs with upsampling factors up to 16x. Then it's tested on 32x upsampling it never saw during training, as well as scenarios with different material properties represented by different coefficient maps. This tests not just the model's capacity to interpolate, but its ability to extrapolate the learned multiscale patterns.

Visual comparison shows the method handles both in-distribution cases (left, upsampling factor 16x) and out-of-distribution extrapolation (right, upsampling factor 32x). The reconstructed field structure remains recognizable even beyond the training regime. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sota_mix.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sota_mix.jpg] Visual comparison shows the method handles both in-distribution cases (left, upsampling factor 16x) and out-of-distribution extrapolation (right, upsampling factor 32x). The reconstructed field structure remains recognizable even beyond the training regime.

The results show the method generalizes reasonably well out-of-distribution, though with some expected degradation as you push further from the training regime. This is the critical finding because it justifies calling this a "learned multiscale correction strategy" rather than just image super-resolution applied to finite element data. The network has learned something about how multiscale structure works in general, not just memorized specific examples.

To understand how the network adapts across different physical scenarios, the approach includes conditioning on material properties. By feeding different coefficient maps to the encoder, the network learns to adjust its multiscale correction strategy based on the physical parameters.

Conditional super-resolution demonstrates that the model adapts its correction pattern based on different coefficient maps and upsampling factors, showing learned flexibility across physical scenarios. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/condition.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/condition.jpg] Conditional super-resolution demonstrates that the model adapts its correction pattern based on different coefficient maps and upsampling factors, showing learned flexibility across physical scenarios.

The network learns that different materials and heterogeneities require different fine-scale correction patterns, and it captures this adaptability in its weights.

WHAT THE NUMBERS ACTUALLY TELL US

At the end, you need empirical validation: is this actually better than alternatives? How much better? The paper compares against other super-resolution methods, other learning approaches like basic neural networks and other implicit neural representation variants, and standard finite element upsampling baselines.

The comparison metrics matter enormously because, as noted earlier, pixel-level error doesn't capture what scientists actually care about. The paper includes both traditional metrics (mean squared error, mean absolute error) and perceptual metrics that measure whether the fine-scale structure aligns with ground truth.

Sliced pixel comparisons show the proposed method follows sharp transitions and fine details more closely than competitors, especially at boundaries and high-frequency regions. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sliced_compare_v3.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sliced_compare_v3.jpg] Sliced pixel comparisons show the proposed method follows sharp transitions and fine details more closely than competitors, especially at boundaries and high-frequency regions.

When you slice specific pixel sequences and compare methods, the proposed approach tracks the ground truth more faithfully than alternatives. Competitors either miss sharp transitions entirely or smear them out, while this method preserves fine structure with fidelity.

Residual visualizations reveal where the improvements are largest.

Residual differences between the proposed method and simpler local implicit transformer baselines show that gains are concentrated in high-frequency regions and sharp transitions. The visualization multiplies residuals by 20 times for visibility, but the pattern is clear: the proposed method reduces errors especially where fine structure matters most, at boundaries and transitions between regions with different properties.

The paper also tests the method on real-world soil pattern data, demonstrating that the learned patterns transfer to actual scientific data beyond the synthetic training regime.

Real-world soil patterns show that the method generalizes to natural spatial heterogeneity, successfully reconstructing fine-scale structure from coarse observations. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/real_world.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/real_world.jpg] Real-world soil patterns show that the method generalizes to natural spatial heterogeneity, successfully reconstructing fine-scale structure from coarse observations.

This connection to real data is important because it grounds the work in practical utility. The method isn't just clever on carefully-curated synthetic examples; it works on the types of data scientists actually encounter.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE NUMBERS

The paper ultimately succeeds because it solves a three-part problem elegantly. First, it reframes multiscale simulation as a learned-pattern problem, replacing hand-derived mathematical relationships with neural network induction from examples. Second, it builds neural network architecture specifically designed for multiscale structure: local implicit representations for continuous spatial prediction, transformers to learn long-range dependencies, and Gabor wavelets to overcome the frequency bias in neural networks. Third, it uses perceptual supervision via stochastic cosine similarity to ensure the learned patterns are physically meaningful, not just mathematically smooth.

The individual components are solid engineering. But their combination creates something genuinely useful: a system that learns a generalizable multiscale correction that works even on unseen scenarios, generating high-frequency details that reflect actual physics rather than neural network artifacts.

For scientists and engineers, this offers a practical advantage. Run expensive multiscale simulations once to train a network. Then use that network to quickly augment fast coarse simulations with plausible fine-scale structure. It's not a replacement for rigorous multiscale mathematics, but it's a powerful complement, trading theoretical guarantees for computational speed and practical effectiveness. In domains like material science, fluid dynamics, and geophysics, where multiscale phenomena dominate and compute resources are finite, this kind of learned correction becomes genuinely valuable.

Today to have a website even for fun, maybe a blog about your dog, you need to take care of many more things, and your site responsiveness is definitely one of them, what is responsiveness you asking? Ok, let's find out it first

The system accepts text descriptions of arbitrary length and complexity, along with optional reference images for conditional generation tasks. The model outputs high-resolution images ranging from 1024x1024 to 2048x1024 pixels, maintaining visual coherence and detail quality across diverse generation scenarios.</p> <h3>Inputs</h3> <ul> <li><strong>Text prompts</strong> describing desired image content, including detailed specifications for layout, composition, and visual elements</li> <li><strong>Reference images</strong> for image-to-image tasks such as editing and style transfer</li> <li><strong>Multiple reference images</strong> for maintaining consistency across subjects in multi-image generation scenarios</li> <li><strong>Guidance parameters</strong> controlling the strength of prompt adherence and generation diversity</li> </ul> <h3>Outputs</h3> <ul> <li><strong>Generated images</strong> in PNG format at specified dimensions</li> <li><strong>High-fidelity visual content</strong> with accurate text rendering and fine-grained details</li> <li><strong>Edited or transformed images</strong> preserving identity and compositional elements from source images</li> </ul> <h2>Capabilities</h2> <p>The model generates images from text descriptions with particular strength in information-dense layouts. Recipe illustrations with ingredient lists, numbered steps, and visual hierarchies render with precise text and accurate proportions. Image-to-image capabilities include background replacement, style transfer between images, identity-preserving generation for people and objects, and multi-subject consistency maintenance. The decoupled reinforcement learning training using the GRPO algorithm enhances both semantic alignment and visual detail quality, with the autoregressive module improving aesthetic understanding and the diffusion decoder refining texture fidelity and text accuracy. Post-training feedback signals target low-frequency features like composition and high-frequency elements like texture, creating nuanced control over output characteristics.</p> <h2>What can I use it for?</h2> <p>Design professionals can generate detailed marketing materials with embedded text and complex layouts without manual typography adjustments. Educational content creators produce recipe cards, instructional guides, and infographics with embedded text that renders correctly on the first attempt. E-commerce businesses create product photography variations with consistent branding and identity. Visual artists explore style transfer to apply artistic treatments while preserving subject identity. items.title: Meta Doesn't Need to Win the AI Race: It Already Owns the Starting Grid
items.author: Benny Doda
items.content:
Muse looks like another AI agent on the surface. When you look closer, you realise it’s a much bigger bet they are making. They are assuming the real prize in AI isn't the smartest model, but the system that knows who you are, understands what you want, and has permission to act on your behalf.

The easiest way to misunderstand Meta's new Muse agent is to treat it as another entrant in the increasingly ridiculous AI model horse race.

OpenAI releases their something-or-other, Anthropic responds, and then Google moves. A benchmark changes and Reddit declares somebody dead, and then X spends 48 hours announcing that one company has achieved AGI and another has become completely irrelevant and we are all cooked. Short race finished, and then everybody moves onto the next race.

Against that background, Muse seemed to arrive rather suddenly. Meta launched it on September 8, and within days it had climbed to the top of the US App Store. Reuters reported 2.8 million downloads in its first 12 days. Muse can manage emails, research purchases, book travel, use financial information, complete transactions, and continue working after you have closed the app. Automation invasion for the normies has finally arrived.

It looked like Zuckerberg had suddenly turned up at the agent party, but if you have been watching closely, he hadn't.

Meta founded its Fundamental AI Research operation in 2013. Meta AI was already embedded inside Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger at scale by the time 2024 finally rolled around. In April 2025, the company launched a standalone Meta AI app specifically designed to remember context and personalise itself using information people had already chosen to share across Meta products. By May that year, Zuckerberg said Meta AI had reached one billion monthly users; how they count that is very interesting. Later in 2025, Meta announced that interactions with its AI products would become another signal used to personalise content and advertising across connected Meta accounts. This is 4D chess right here.

Then came Muse Spark, Meta's new model family, followed by agentic capabilities that connected Meta AI to email and calendars and allowed it to make plans and complete work. Muse is not the beginning of that story; it’s just the thing that makes you take notice when they deemed it was the right time. I think a lot of the AI industry is still looking at the wrong scoreboard.

The model race matters. It just might not matter as much as we think.

For the one percent of users who spend their lives switching between Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok, Kimi, and whatever was released last Thursday, model performance matters enormously. They notice a five-point coding improvement; they change subscriptions because an agent suddenly became better at spreadsheets. Most of the planet doesn’t behave like this; they are the exception.’

Meta's Family of Apps averaged 3.6 billion daily users in June. In the second quarter of 2026, the company generated $60.8 billion in revenue, of which $59.36 billion came from advertising. That means roughly 97.6% of Meta's quarterly revenue still came from ads. I recently wrote about Amazon banning access to agents on its platform. It fundamentally ruins the platform economics for Amazon, as they do $68 billion a year in advertising revenue, approximately 9.57% of their total revenue.

That matters because Meta has spent twenty years becoming extraordinarily good at one particular problem: understanding what gets us human beings to look at something, click something, share something, buy something, or come back tomorrow. AI is now making that machine better.

Meta told investors that Instagram time spent grew by double digits year-on-year in the second quarter, largely because of improvements in ‘Feed and Reels’ recommendations. Facebook video time increased 9% globally. Meta says its newer recommendation architecture draws on deeper user history, while its LLMs increasingly analyse content, interests and past interactions to improve predictions about what individual users will care about next.

Zuckerberg was explicit about the advantage during Meta's earnings call. He described Meta as a company that builds consumer products reaching billions of people and, once something works, knows how to scale it to an enormous audience.

That may be the part of the AI race Silicon Valley keeps underestimating, and why I think Meta could still be hugely underrated as a stock, because the best model can win a benchmark, but distribution wins Tuesday morning.

Muse doesn't just want prompts. It needs context.

For a personal agent to actually be useful, it can’t know only what you typed into a chatbot yesterday. It needs to know your calendar, your email, what you bought, where you need to be, what your partner told you, which flight you booked, what you can afford, which people matter to you, and which things you always forget.

Meta's own Muse page encourages users to connect email, calendars, Instagram and other everyday apps. Its Mac application can, with permission, work with files, Messages, Calendar, and Notes. Plaid is providing connections to financial accounts so Muse can offer personalised financial assistance. Meta says 1Password integration is coming. There are more than 2000 connected integrations already. That sounds terrifying when you write it as a list, but it also sounds exactly like what a useful personal agent would need.

And this is where I think Meta deserves more credit than some of the current commentary gives it. Muse runs inside a dedicated secure virtual machine, and they say credentials are stored separately so the model itself can’t see them. Sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase require approval so at least there is an audit trail.

Users apparently can control individual connections. Meta says Muse conversations and the data stored in the VM are not passed to its advertising systems, and a more strongly encrypted Confidential VM is planned in which even Meta would not be able to access the contents.

Those are not trivial protections, but they do not make the strategic implication any smaller. Because Meta does not need to secretly shove your Gmail inbox into an advertising model for Muse to become enormously valuable to Meta. It merely needs Muse to become the place where you go when you want something done. That is why they are running a different race at the moment.

This is where the burner-account problem gets weird.

We have spent the last decade learning to fragment ourselves online.

There is the work email, personal email, spam email, and the email created because some website demanded one. There is the public Instagram, and then the private Instagram and the account you use to look at things you would rather not train your public algorithm on.

Meta itself recognised this behaviour years ago; yep, they were all over it. Facebook now allows users to create up to four additional personal profiles under their main account specifically so different interests and communities can remain separate and, of course, not to tie your alter egos to yourself. WhatsApp can remain separate from Meta's broader account system, although users can voluntarily connect it. In 2026, Meta began rolling Accounts Center into a broader Meta Account designed to manage apps and devices under one identity system. That all makes sense in the social-media era, but… the agent era creates the opposite incentive.

A privacy-conscious user may decide to give an AI agent a secondary email address, a limited calendar, a burner profile, and only a carefully sanitised slice of their life. I know I do it that way. But I’m continually told that every layer of separation makes the agent slightly more stupid.

It can’t remind you about the restaurant reservation buried in the other inbox. It can’t realise that tomorrow's meeting conflicts with the dentist because the dentist is on another calendar. It can’t understand that the person emailing you is the same person appearing in your WhatsApp conversations. It cannot optimise your spending if it only sees one account, and it certainly can’t see that you’ve already dated and blocked that one person on another dating app.

So we are heading towards a fascinating identity problem. At what point does the account you trust with your inbox, calendar, relationships, purchases, finances, and personal history become your real account? Are these becoming a series of best on which combination and stack works best? I certainly don’t want to get arrested in 20 years for trading Lima beans on a black-market lookmaxxing site, because unlike burner email accounts, burner agent-connected accounts decide they want to ‘live on’.

Maybe the future "real account" isn't Facebook, Google, an email address, etc.; maybe it is an agent. The account with the richest authenticated context about you and permission to operate on your behalf may eventually matter more than the hundred accounts sitting underneath it, but hey, that’s a very different internet.

And then there is the slightly absurd AI contradiction.

For several years, the public has simultaneously been told that artificial intelligence may be the most dangerous technology humanity has ever created. This whole AI doomer thing is already getting old, but it’s certainly occupying its fair share of space on mediums like the dying New York Times.

Researchers discuss alignment and Governments discuss catastrophic risk. AI companies publish preparedness frameworks and meltdown philosophical crisis papers, thinly veiled and geared toward regulatory capture. Meta's own Advanced AI Scaling Framework explicitly evaluates risks including cyber capabilities, biological threats, and potential loss of control.

Then the consumer product arrives and essentially says, hold my beer, I’m going to need access to all the things you use, own, frequent, and operate, and I want to be able to fill things out, buy things, work while you are asleep, and do all the things that could actually expedite the very thing that feeds the fears.

That contrast is one of the most bonkers things I have seen in my ample years on the blue marble.

I don't necessarily think it is a bad thing. In fact, I suspect ordinary consumers may eventually reach a more pragmatic conclusion about AI than much of the industry has. People have always traded some degree of control for enough utility. We gave smartphones our locations because maps became useful. We gave cloud services our photographs because having every photograph on every device was useful.

We stored our credit cards in browsers because typing sixteen digits repeatedly became annoying. Agents will probably cross the same line. Let’s face it, we are VERY good at creating lies to ourselves about those trade-offs, and we are excellent at saying, “ah, it will be OK”.

But it is entirely reasonable for someone to look at the wider AI safety conversation and ask why, if the machines are supposedly one capability jump away from becoming HAL 9000, the onboarding screen would ask permission to access their bank account. The industry has never completely reconciled those two messages, and Meta is simply making the contradiction visible.

Zuckerberg may have learned which race actually matters.

There is another reason I think Muse matters. Zuckerberg has spoken openly about Meta's historic strategic weakness: it did not control the dominant computing platforms underneath its products.

In a 2025 conversation with Stripe co-founder John Collison, Zuckerberg said that if Meta arrived at the next computing platform at roughly the same time as Apple, Google or Microsoft, the incumbents would have the advantage because they already possessed the underlying ecosystem. His conclusion was that Meta needed to be earlier and better.

That helps explain the enormous investment in glasses, and it also somewhat helps to explain Muse.

Yesterday Meta announced that Muse is coming to its AI glasses. The progression starts to make sense: social graph, messaging, recommendation engine, AI assistant, personal agent, persistent identity, then an ambient hardware device that can see and hear the world alongside you.

Meta isn’t gunning for the best chatbot; they are trying very hard not to spend the next computing era living inside somebody else's operating system. So all eyes are on attention.

The moat can’t be only about data. It is the feedback loop.

People often say Meta possesses enormous amounts of data, which is obviously true but not particularly insightful because we all know the more important advantage is what happens to the data after it arrives.

Meta sees enormous volumes of human behavior. Its models use that behavior to improve recommendations, because better recommendations increase engagement and more engagement creates more behavioral signals. Those signals improve advertising and personalization, and then those improvements attract businesses and creators, who create more things for people to interact with, and now they are putting a personal agent inside that loop.

Meta has already said interactions with Meta AI can be used as another recommendation signal across connected Meta accounts. Ask Meta AI about hiking and, under the policy introduced in 2025, that interest can help shape the content and ads you see elsewhere within the Meta ecosystem. Muse itself, ‘they say,’ is treated differently; Meta says its VM data and conversations are not shared with the ad system, but the broader strategic direction toward AI-mediated personalisation could hardly be clearer.

The doomers will be quick to state that Meta built an AI to steal more information about you. There really isn't evidence for that claim.

The flip-side version would be that Meta has built an AI that becomes more useful the more accurately it understands you, while Meta already owns one of the largest identity, attention, and distribution networks ever constructed.

I, for one, don’t need to be tricked into giving it context, but I have to make a decision on whether the utility of the offering is great enough for me to volunteer my information. That is a much better business for them to run, and a much smarter race to try and win.

This is the 4D chess move.

Muse may become the world's dominant personal agent, or, yeah, it may not.

Google has some very tip-top advantages of its own, and OpenAI has massive consumer mindshare. Anthropic is strong in professional and enterprise workflows, and Apple controls some of the world's most valuable consumer hardware. Personal agents remain unreliable, security is difficult, and consumer trust is far from guaranteed.

Meta's not-so-squeaky-clean history means some people will quite rationally be more cautious about handing it access to sensitive information. Reuters reported this week that even an experimental Muse feature using human contractors to complete some phone calls generated internal privacy concerns.

Meta doesn’t need to win over all the Frontier-AI obsessed people and declare Muse the winner. The people swapping models every fortnight are interesting, vocal and disproportionately visible online. They are not three and a half billion people.

Meta's advantage is that it already knows how to reach everybody else and in a language they all understand.

The company can survive losing a benchmark or a model arriving six weeks late. It can survive somebody on X declaring its AI strategy dead before breakfast. It has done something similar through mobile, Stories, Reels, messaging, short-form video and multiple rounds of technological panic. It is a king of dying fast and not skipping a beat.

What it can’t afford is to lose control of the interface through which billions of ordinary people encounter the next generation of computing. Muse suggests Zuckerberg understands that perfectly.

The only question that will ever matter is who owns the relationship between the intelligence and the human being using it.

And, eventually, which account the human considers to be the one that actually represents them. If that becomes the real AI race, Meta didn't arrive late at all because it’s been standing on the starting grid for twenty years.

items.title: Publishing on HackerNoon Is a Badge You Get to Keep
items.author: Editing Protocol
items.content:
A few weeks ago, we came across a video from a developer walking through the CV that helped take him from Lagos to London.

His name is Pleasant Balogun. He started coding as a teenager, built his first tools using his mom’s Android phone, launched products, had companies acquire his work, and eventually qualified for the UK’s Global Talent route.

But there was one small part of his story that caught our attention.

Back in 2021, Pleasant won HackerNoon Contributor of the Year for Developer Tools.

Looking back on it in his video, Pleasant said the recognition “contributed to… everything downstream.” He then went on to talk about the projects, companies, acquisitions, and experience that eventually formed the application that took him to London.

Now, before anyone starts rewriting their immigration plans around their HackerNoon profile: we are not saying a HackerNoon award got Pleasant his UK visa.

He doesn’t say that either.

What his story does show is something we think writers sometimes underestimate:

Putting your work somewhere credible creates receipts.

Anyone can create a HackerNoon account and submit a story, but not every submission makes it to publication. Every story goes through editorial review, and as we’ve written before, roughly 60% of the stories that enter our editorial queue don’t make the cut.

That selectivity matters because when you publish something useful, technical, original, or genuinely insightful, you’re doing more than adding another post to the internet. You’re creating a public record of what you knew, what you built, what you believed, or the problems you could solve at a particular point in your career.

That record can take on different forms of value over time. Six months later, it might be something you send to a recruiter; two years later, it could help establish your expertise; and five years later, it might sit in your portfolio alongside the projects, jobs, awards, conference talks, and open-source contributions you’ve accumulated along the way.

You rarely know which piece of work will matter most in the future, and Pleasant probably didn’t either.

Look Around at Who You’re Publishing Next To

There’s another part of publishing on HackerNoon that’s easy to miss when you’re staring at an empty draft: the community you’re joining.

That’s the community you’re entering when you hit submit: not one where every writer works at Microsoft, Amazon, or the next billion-dollar startup, and certainly not one where job titles automatically make someone’s ideas better. HackerNoon has always been a place for people building technology to explain what they’re seeing, often before the rest of the industry has completely caught up.

You might be reading an engineer solving a production problem at massive scale, a founder building a company nobody has heard of yet, or a 17-year-old creating something on his mom’s phone. The point is that you don’t always know who someone is going to become, and you don’t need to know their title to recognize that they have something worth sharing.

Publish Before You Think You’re “Qualified”

This is probably the bigger lesson: a lot of people wait until they have the impressive title, the successful startup, the senior role, or the decade of experience before they feel qualified to write publicly. But building a body of work is often what helps them get there in the first place.

Write about something you built, explain the weird bug you spent three days solving, or document an experiment that failed. Make the argument everyone on your team keeps having, or share a technical decision you’d make differently today. Your first article doesn’t need to establish you as the world’s foremost expert; it just needs to show that you have something real to contribute.

That work can compound in unexpected ways. A side project becomes a job interview, a GitHub repository catches the attention of a founder, or an article becomes proof that you understood a technology years before it became fashionable. Even a HackerNoon award can become a line on your CV that’s still worth talking about five years later.

You can’t predict where any of this will lead, but you can give your work a better chance of being discovered by putting it somewhere people can find it.

So, if you’ve been sitting on an idea because you don’t think your name is big enough yet, remember that the people whose names seem big today had to publish their first piece somewhere, too.

Want to take this further? (HackerNoon’s Blogging Course)

HackerNoon’s Blogging Course is designed for beginners  writers who’ve published a bit and want to level up. It’s organized into 8 modules created by experienced writers and editors, and it includes topics like:

Until next time, Hackers! 💚
