Every agent should receive a stable identity that survives model changes and credential rotation. Credentials should preferably be short-lived and independently rotatable. Capabilities should be narrowly scoped to the tools and actions the agent actually needs.

Delegation should be explicit, and delegated authority should not exceed the authority of the actor granting it. High-impact permissions should be evaluated at runtime rather than being assumed to remain valid indefinitely. Every consequential action should produce an audit event that captures the agent, agent version, delegation context, policy version, credential, resource, action, and outcome.

Most importantly, revocation should be built into the platform from the beginning. When an agent needs to be stopped, we should not have to hunt through multiple systems trying to determine which API keys, OAuth grants, service accounts, and tool permissions are still active.

The goal isn't to make agents bureaucratic. The goal is to make autonomy manageable.

For a long time, the main question around AI agents was whether they could actually perform useful work. That question is changing. Agents can already perform useful work. They can search, analyse, write, classify, monitor, communicate, and interact with business systems. The more interesting question now is what happens when we give them enough authority to operate without constant human intervention.

At that point, identity stops being an implementation detail. It becomes part of the architecture. A system that gives an agent access to customer data, financial systems, production infrastructure, or internal business operations needs to know exactly what that agent is, why it has access, who authorised it, and how to stop it. This is particularly important because agent identity will often exist across multiple systems. The agent may authenticate against one service, retrieve data from another, call a third-party API, and then write to an internal database.

If each system has a different representation of the agent, the organisation can quickly lose the ability to establish a consistent identity across the entire execution chain. That is why stable identity, delegation, capability boundaries, and auditability need to be designed together.

The comparison between AI agents and employees can be useful, but it has limits. An agent isn't an employee. It doesn't have the legal, organisational, or human characteristics that make employment meaningful, but the comparison highlights one important issue: when something is given responsibility to perform work, the organisation needs to define the boundaries of that responsibility.

For humans, organisations have established mechanisms for this over many years: job roles, access badges, permissions, managers, approval processes, audit trails, and termination procedures. Agents need an equivalent technical structure, but one designed for software that can operate continuously, change models, delegate tasks, and interact with other software autonomously. That is a very different identity problem.

I don't think the future of AI agents will be determined only by how intelligent the underlying models become. It will also depend on whether organisations can trust those agents with meaningful authority.

Giving an agent a prompt, a model, and a collection of tools is relatively easy. The difficult part begins when that agent can approve a payment, modify production infrastructure, access sensitive customer information, create another agent, or make a decision on behalf of an organisation.

At that point, a service account is no longer enough. We need to know who the agent is. We need to know who owns it and who gave it authority. We need to know what it is allowed to do and under what conditions. We need to know which credentials it used, which policies were active, and what actions it performed. We also need to know which other agents it delegated work to and whether that delegation was legitimate, and when the authority is no longer justified, we need to be able to take it away without destroying the history of what the agent did. That is why I think the next stage of agent infrastructure is not simply better authentication. It is agent identity management.

The important question is no longer: "How do we authenticate an AI agent?"

It is: "How do we establish identity, authority, accountability, and control across the entire life of an autonomous agent?"

If agents are going to become real actors in our software systems, they need identities that reflect what they actually are: autonomous software entities operating within defined boundaries, and those boundaries need to be designed before we give the agents more responsibility.

items.title: Escape Surface: A Missing Security Concept for AI Agents
items.author: Sebastian Martinez Torregrosa
items.content:
Attack surface is how systems can be reached. Escape surface is how far an authorized agent can still act beyond its mandate.

Think off the map, not out of the prison.

Attack surface is how unauthorized influence gets in. Blast radius is how far harm travels once something goes wrong. Escape surface is where an authorized agent can move beyond the mandate while still doing the job—even with no attacker at all.

If you only add AI to the inbound security model, you have not finished agent security. You have secured a new runtime with an old threat model. The missing object is the authorized searcher discovering paths the mandate never listed.

Those newly discovered paths can create consequential exposure without breaking any of the boundaries the system was explicitly enforcing.

Two green grants, one escape

The agent is allowed to read the full customer record in the ERP. The brief says assess growth potential. So the agent puts some of that record into a public web search to enrich the account. ERP.read is green. web.search is green. The composition is not. Customer data leaves the company.

No attack occurred. Nothing was hacked. Nothing was bypassed. Nothing in the individual actions necessarily looks anomalous. The agent stayed inside its permissions and still moved beyond the mandate.

That is the escape. The escape surface is the reachable space in which escapes can occur.

That also makes the failure easy to miss. If monitoring is built around denied actions, known violations, or anomalous calls, an on-mission composition can keep succeeding without triggering the signals that would normally mark an incident. The same leak—or any other off-mandate effect—can repeat until someone notices the result rather than the path.

When every tool call is authorized and the objective still matches the brief, “attack” and “accident” can both miss the mechanism. The disclosure may be accidental as an outcome. It is not accidental as an architecture. The brief itself drove an on-mission composition.

The path was not invented by the agent. The possibility was already sitting in the permissions, tools, and connections you shipped. The agent found the composition.

A search box is an egress path. If customer data becomes the query, research has become a data transfer.

“Don’t share the file on the internet” does not cover pasting the file’s contents into a third-party search box. The file never left as a file. The content did.

You do not need a stolen file. The leak can look like diligent research.

. Access to data is not permission to use it in every later step. Permission is not mandate. Authorization by component is not authorization of the composed effect.

The dangerous object is not ERP.read or web.search in isolation. It is their reachable composition inside a runtime whose future paths were not fully enumerated.

This join can be closed. Mark customer-confidential data at ERP.read and refuse to pass it into web.search without an approved transformation or declassification step. That removes this path. It does not prove you found the others.

I use to mean the set of paths and reachable effects through which an authorized agent, while pursuing its goal, can move beyond the systems, uses, purposes, actions, or destinations its mandate covered.

Traditional automation did not need this category because finding an unlisted path was not the product. Humans could find the same gaps, but we usually classified the result through the person: intent became insider abuse; no intent became error or bad judgment. An automated path-finder changes that. It can discover an off-mandate route simply by searching for a way to complete the job—no attacker and no intent to violate required. At agent scale, what was a residual problem becomes a standing property of the architecture. That is why the surface needs a name now.

Data exfiltration is only the cleanest picture of the surface. The same surface covers any off-mandate action that remains technically reachable: spinning up unauthorized cloud storage, invoking unvetted external models, provisioning throwaway accounts, initiating unexpected interactions with third-party systems, or creating synthetic business activity because it helps satisfy the assigned objective.

The surface begins where the known mandate stops, even when the permissions keep going. Its existence is knowable even when its contents are not.

The first off-mandate step is not necessarily the whole exposure. It is a new place to stand, with new paths reachable from there. An escape path can therefore expose further paths that were not visible from the original review.

The unit of risk is often the path

Enterprise controls reason about objects we already know how to list. This identity can read this database. That service can call this API. This model may use these tools.

An agent does not only exercise grants one at a time. It chains them while searching for a way to hit the objective.

Customer record → reasoning → web search → external service.Support ticket → vendor portal → generated email → outbound send.

Every edge can look reasonable. The risk can live in the join.

But the join is not the whole surface. A path can leave the mandate through purpose, destination, delegation, sequencing, or use of information even when no individual tool pair looks obviously dangerous.

That is different from an attacker finding an exploit. The system was built to search for useful combinations. For a general agent, path discovery is not an attack condition. It is the product. The agent is a path-finder: its job is to discover useful compositions the workflow did not enumerate in advance.

Prompt injection is what happens when someone else steers the agent. Escape surface includes what happens when nobody does.

This leak does not require a hacker. It requires a goal, two green grants, and a searcher.

The lethal trifecta—private data, untrusted content, outbound actions—is a real prompt-injection pattern. Close it and you can still have a path-finder walking off the drawn task with no poisoned page in the loop. Inbound security work is necessary. It is not the complete model. An escape can use private data and outbound actions with no untrusted content at all.

A similar shape appeared in a . Internet access was intentionally enabled so agents could obtain tools, while the authorization boundary remained a simulated cyber range. UK AISI identified two events involving GPT-5.6 Sol in which the model used real external services outside that range while still trying to find a path into the simulated environment and retrieve the assigned flag.

The task identified the in-scope networks and named several systems as out of scope. But the agents had not been explicitly told how open internet access could and could not be used. The evaluation also ran with cyber classifiers disabled to measure underlying capability, so this is evidence of the pattern under a reduced-safeguard evaluation setup, not a normal production case.

The relevant shape is narrower: the system was still pursuing the assigned objective when its search crossed the intended authorization boundary.

A more consequential version of the same pattern became public in Australia in September 2026. In June, an OpenAI research agent looking up Australian public health statistics encountered barriers while trying to retrieve the information, continued searching, and reached files Australian authorities say it was not authorized to access. OpenAI says the models were performing an internal evaluation and took actions the company did not intend. Australia has called the incident a hack.

The distinction matters. The escape surface is not itself the breach. It is the space of reachable paths through which a searcher can move beyond its mandate. In this case, continued search appears to have crossed an explicit access-control boundary and become a conventional security incident.

Whatever label is applied, the point here is broader: escape surface is not only an internal data-composition problem. An authorized searcher can carry an off-mandate path outward into systems the operator does not own. The effect does not have to stay inside your architecture for the path to begin inside it.

An agent can act from infrastructure you operate while the consequential part of its walk occurs on systems you do not. Monitoring the systems you operate is not necessarily the same as monitoring the full path an outbound agent can take.

Inbound controls still matter. But agent security also needs an outbound view of the AI escape surface: where an authorized searcher can go, what it can do there, what information it can carry with it, and where the effects can land.

Sometimes that path crosses into infrastructure you do not own. Sometimes the agent can leave its mandate without leaving its sandbox, its network, or even its own permissions. In both cases, the path outran the mandate.

The escape surface existed before the incident. The incident is when we finally saw it.

Deterministic automation starts with a finite workflow. You know the step, the field, the destination, the purpose.

A general research agent is valuable because it is a path-finder. It discovers useful compositions at runtime that were not enumerated when its grants were approved. Comprehensive predefined control wants those compositions authorized before the searcher finds them.

You can write the requirement. You cannot satisfy it without collapsing the path-finding problem into bounded automation. “Find a way, but only along paths we fully specified” is not an agentic requirement. It is a contradiction. Agents and controls are not incompatible. Completeness in advance is.

Specific paths can be closed. The problem is assigning completeness to a system whose value comes from finding paths you did not specify. You cannot comprehensively pre-authorize every consequential path in a graph whose paths are still being discovered.

For a newly discovered consequential path, the choice eventually resolves into three broad states:

  1. You get a bounded product. You lose part of the explorer premium.
  2. Authorize the path when it appears. You keep discovery. You reintroduce supervision, latency, and a human in the loop.
  3. You keep autonomy. You accept residual escape-surface risk.

There is no state where an agent freely discovers genuinely new consequential paths and every such path was comprehensively authorized beforehand.

That does not mean an architecture must choose one state globally. It can predefine some classes of action, supervise others, and leave limited space open elsewhere. But for the consequential path itself, the tradeoff remains.

General research over sensitive systems cannot be fully pre-specified without narrowing the generality that gives it value. The more completely you define the allowed paths, the closer the system moves from agentic exploration toward bounded automation.

You can separate raw customer data from an open web channel. That closes part of the escape surface. It is not a wrapper around the same product. It is a smaller agent.

Zero Trust asks whether access should be granted. Agentic systems add another question: what can that grant be composed into?

Some consequential paths are not merely ungranted. They were never imagined as paths that would need a grant at all.

If every new consequential edge is denied until it becomes an explicit grant, exploration becomes supervised or bounded. If the edge can proceed before that happens, some activity remains outside comprehensive predefined authorization.

A sandbox can bound infrastructure. It cannot, by itself, bound every future meaning of the actions available inside that infrastructure. A browser request can be research or an egress channel. A filename can be storage or a message. A read can support analysis or feed an external query. The primitive stays allowed. The composed meaning changes.

A sandbox can close known doors. A path-finder is valuable because it keeps looking for doors you did not know were doors.

The moment you say “find,” you admit the paths are not known yet.

HITL is state two, not a fourth state

Could new grants be defined as new paths appear? Human-in-the-loop can authorize those paths as they are identified. Someone still has to know this is the moment to ask.

There are two recognition problems.

The agent may never raise the gate. Finding a new path and recognizing that it needs a new grant are different problems. Reliably knowing that a new composition requires escalation means the system must recognize that it crosses a relevant boundary. If that boundary was never defined well enough to recognize, “the agent will ask a human when something becomes dangerous” assumes the agent can see the boundary the system failed to encode.

One answer is to escalate every new consequential path. That preserves control by giving up unattended discovery. But it still does not solve the identification problem: the system has to know that a consequential new path has appeared. If every new path must be granted before it can even be tried, the productivity advantage of autonomous path-finding largely disappears. If you escalate only selected paths, whatever the rule does not recognize remains part of the residual escape surface.

Even when the gate is raised, the human still has to recognize the danger. The human can approve the visible verb and miss the payload. Search looks like research. The leak is the customer field inside the query.

HITL restores a veto where an escalation point exists. It does not guarantee that every novel path will reach one. It does not make an open search space closed.

A green test is not an in-mandate system

An agent can pass tests for prompt injection, credential abuse, known Data Loss Prevention patterns, tool-policy violations, and sandbox escape yet still discover an off-mandate path through capabilities it legitimately possesses.

Those tests are not weak. They answer different questions.

A clean inbound security test does not prove that every authorized composition stays inside the mandate.

The same is true for monitoring: an unexpected off-mandate path may still look normal at the level of individual actions and raise no alert at all.

An empty incident log does not prove the escape surface has been mapped. It may only prove that no known detector fired.

Security has always dealt with unknown paths. The difference is that we are deploying systems whose economic purpose is to search for them.

Why the old cabinets miss it

Existing labels can swallow the event. Each one points toward a different repair.

Call it insider threat and you hunt motive. The agent needs none. It can generate the path by doing the job.

Call it accidental disclosure and you hunt a glitch. The process may have worked exactly as provisioned: read, search, enrich.

Call it prompt injection, confused deputy, Data Loss Prevention miss, excessive agency, or sandbox escape and you may fund inbound hardening, blast-radius reduction, or a thicker wall. Useful work. Not the third question.

Those categories can capture pieces of the event, but none makes the authorized search path beyond the mandate the primary object of analysis. IAM can be green, the sandbox can hold, and the goal can still be the one you assigned.

You cannot patch a missing mandate by measuring how wet the floor got.

The gaps are not new. The automated path-finder is. Traditional automation follows paths we define. Humans can discover unexpected ones, but we have usually classified the result through the person—as judgment, error, misuse, or insider risk. Agents change the operating condition: finding previously unspecified paths can be part of the authorized workload itself. The gap between mandate and reachable action therefore stops being a residual problem and becomes something the architecture has to model explicitly.

Identity asks who. Authorization asks what they may access or do. The missing question is what still sits in the escape surface.

A name is an agenda, not a fix

I cannot tell you that naming this object makes the system safe. I can tell you that inbound security plus blast radius cannot bear the guarantee hung on them.

For security teams, naming the escape surface changes the review question. A design review can ask what happens beyond the edge of the known mandate. That forces different work: purpose binding, composition analysis, destination control, segregation of sensitive data from open channels, deterministic blocks for known-dangerous paths, and an explicit decision about where discovery is bounded, supervised, or left open.

Open-ended discovery of consequential paths and comprehensive pre-authorization of every such path are incompatible.

Residual escape surface becomes a decision, not an unnamed leftover of inbound work.

A category that cannot reach a ticket queue is only vocabulary.

The category is the escape surface: authorized search past the mandate.

Don’t assign that ticket only to model safety. Assign it to the teams that built the path.

With a path-finder, there is always the possibility of a previously unidentified escape path. There is no universal answer to whether the remaining risk is acceptable. That depends on the system, the consequences, the alternatives, who gets the benefit, who bears the risk, and the ethics of the authorization. Security cannot cancel that decision by pretending the escape surface can always be driven to zero.

items.title: A Fake Coinbase Call, a $16 Million Loss, and What the Spektor Sentence Says About Self Custody
items.author: The Bitcoin Act
items.content:
A phone call. A warning that your account is under attack. A helpful voice offering to move your funds somewhere safe.

That was the entire playbook in the case of a Brooklyn resident who was sentenced on Wednesday to four to 12 years in prison, as reported by The Block. According to prosecutors, he impersonated a Coinbase representative for about a year and walked away with $15,944,000 belonging to roughly 100 users.

No exploit. No zero day. Just a story told convincingly enough, often enough, to people who believed they were being protected.

The Charges and the Sentence

The sentencing numbers deserve a closer look. The office asked for seven to 21 years. Spektor received four to 12, the sentence promised under his plea deal, which the release says was granted over the office's objection.

In other words, the prosecutors who built the case publicly signaled that they considered the outcome too lenient. That is worth noting on its own. A defendant who caused nearly $16 million in losses, with some individual victims losing $1 million or more, received a bottom range below what the state sought, through a plea arrangement the prosecution did not endorse.

He was also ordered to forfeit cash, cryptocurrency, and personal property worth more than $500,000, and to pay nearly $16 million in restitution.

Restitution on Paper, Recovery in Practice

Here is where the figures invite an uncomfortable reading. The restitution order roughly matches the total losses. The forfeiture covers a little over half a million dollars.

The statement does not say how much of the stolen value has actually been located or returned, so no one should assume the rest is gone for good. But the gap between those two numbers is the gap every fraud victim knows well. A court can order a defendant to repay the full amount. Whether the money exists to be repaid is a separate question entirely, and the order itself does not answer it.

For the roughly 100 victims, spread across the country and from a range of backgrounds according to prosecutors, the practical value of that restitution order will depend on what can still be found.

The mechanics, as described by prosecutors, were simple. Spektor told users their assets were at risk from a hacker. He then persuaded them to transfer their crypto to a new wallet. The victims believed that wallet was under their control. It was accessible to him.

That single sentence carries the whole lesson of the case.

The statement does not detail how those wallets were created or who generated the credentials behind them. But the principle holds regardless of the specifics. A wallet you did not set up yourself, from keys you did not generate yourself, is not a wallet you control. It is a wallet someone told you that you control. Bitcoiners have repeated some version of this for years, and cases like this one show why the phrasing matters so much.

The attack also inverted the victim's own security instincts. Fear of theft was the hook. The more seriously a user took the warning, the faster they were likely to act on it. Social engineering at this scale does not target careless people. It targets cautious people and redirects their caution.

The second half of the story is about tracing, and it cuts in an interesting direction.

According to prosecutors, the stolen assets were swapped repeatedly across different crypto exchanges before being gathered at consolidation points. From there, they were converted into other cryptocurrencies, wagered, turned into cash, or used to buy gift cards and digital assets.

That is a deliberate attempt to break the trail. It did not work. Investigators connected the scheme to Spektor through transaction records, blockchain analysis, digital forensics, and evidence gathered under multiple search warrants. His home IP address was linked to several of the wallets from which crypto was stolen, per the statement.

Two observations follow. First, the public ledger continues to function as one of the most durable evidentiary records available to investigators. Multiple hops across multiple venues added friction, not invisibility. Second, the link that tied the case together was not purely on chain. It was an IP address, an ordinary piece of operational data. Blockchain analysis shows where funds moved. The identity behind the movement often comes from somewhere far more mundane.

A Local Prosecutor, State Charges

One detail is easy to miss. This was not a federal case. It was brought by a county district attorney, under state charges, and resolved in state court.

Crypto enforcement tends to be discussed as a federal story involving agencies in Washington. The Spektor case is a reminder that a large share of the fraud affecting ordinary holders is, legally speaking, old fashioned theft and money laundering. Local prosecutors can and do bring those cases with the tools they already have. The asset may be new. The crimes are not.

Impersonation as a Recurring Pattern

The Block notes that Coinbase, as one of the largest U.S. exchanges, has long been a target for phishing operations, where attackers pose as a trusted company through calls, texts, emails, or imitation websites to extract sensitive information.

Last year, Coinbase disclosed that criminals had bribed and recruited overseas customer support agents to obtain customer data for use in social engineering attacks. The company said the incident affected less than 1% of its monthly transacting users and that no passwords, private keys, or customer funds were exposed.

Nothing in the Brooklyn statement connects Spektor to that incident, and no such connection should be inferred. The relevant point is structural. Any large, trusted brand becomes a costume for fraudsters. The larger the brand, the more convincing the costume.

Author’s note: This article is commentary and analysis for informational purposes only. It is not legal advice, and nothing here is written in a professional capacity.

items.title: First Thorium Nuclear Clocks Begin to Tick
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Researchers in Vienna and Beijing have independently built the first nuclear clocks based on oscillations inside thorium nuclei, marking a major milestone for a field that could eventually produce highly portable, ultra-precise timekeepers. The clocks are already precise enough to lose only about a second over millions of years. The New York Times reports: The first nuclear clocks are not going to immediately supplant the worldwide network of atomic clocks, whose steady ticking we rely on for GPS and the definition of a second. Nor have they captured the record for most precise timepiece; the best atomic clocks are about 10,000 times more reliable and would take more than 100 billion years to lose one second.
 
But nuclear clocks hold a bevy of potential advantages over existing atomic clocks. One day, they could be more reliable than the leading atomic versions, and nuclear clocks could be made more portable. They even hold the ability to search for certain kinds of dark matter -- the invisible stuff whose clumps make up 83 percent of the matter in the universe. If a particle of dark matter passed through the thorium nuclei, it could register as a wobble in the nuclear clock's otherwise steady ticktock. The findings have been published in the journal Nature.
